utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. I apologise for the delay. There was some problem. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency. Good morning, Your Excellencies. Good morning to all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ruez. Please help us understand a few more facts and shed light on them. In the transcript of January 26, on page 23709, from lines 1 through 5, you said: [In English] "I was initially in a team investigating the siege of Sarajevo, and in July 1995, as soon as the enclave fell, I was tasked to go in the area and start investigation that was connected with the press rumours about the disappearance of thousands of men, and I never stopped working on this investigation till my departure in April 19 -- 2001." [Interpretation] So you investigated Sarajevo before the fall of Srebrenica, and you were there before the fall of Srebrenica; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not exactly right. I was in the team investigating Sarajevo, but we did not go in the field to conduct any investigation, as long as -- as far as I am concerned, before the month of October or November 1995 where I was during three weeks not working on the Srebrenica case since I was with the Sarajevo team in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On page 23977, from 19 through 25, you say: "The goal of the investigation I was in charge of was to determine the fate of some 8.000 missing after the fall of UN safe area Srebrenica. Therefore, the investigation, that is to say started 11th of July, 12.00, approximately 12.00. Knowing about the general frame of the war, its causes and all the rest, it is indeed something helpful in order to have what one can tell the big picture, but it was certainly not any of the goals of the specific investigation."

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct with one additional precision is that at the time, the precise number was not known. This number came once the ICRC book on all the missing -- missing persons from former Yugoslavia went out, and this number of 8.000 was then determined since it was the rough number of those declared missing from precisely the July 1995 event. For the rest, I don't feel the need to change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the investigation started on the 11th of July. That remains. How many times was this figure changed? How many duplicates were there, that Red Cross list, and how many corrections were made to that effect?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the bit about investigations started on 11th July, I already provided previously an answer on this, so I have to repeat. It's not that the investigation started on 11th July. The investigation -- the starting points of the events under investigation are the events that started from 11th July and all the dates after 11th July. So in this case, mainly between 11th July and 17 July. This is the -- the -- these are the dates of the -- of the events under investigation, knowing that the end date 7 July is a date that we learned only later on, because the 17th of July is the end of the burial process of the people who had been executed on the location determined by the investigation. For the rest, you had some questions. Let me return to them. Yeah, the book of the Red Cross, the ICRC book. I don't know how many -- how many of these -- of this list how many samples have been spread. I have no idea. How many times it might have changed, I don't know if there has been any change later on. We had an expert of -- in demography who testified during the trial of Krstic. He would be the one who could provide all the details about the list of those declared missing from July 1995. Yes, this is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So on page 23977, what it says there would not be correct, right, what it says between lines 19 and 25, namely that the investigation started at midday on the 11th of July; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Again, what I said is that I arrived together with one additional investigator in Tuzla area. I think it was 20 July. So this is the starting date of the investigation, but the events under investigation are the events that happened in the enclave at -- starting at 11th July around 12.00 -- around 12.00 being the bombing that sparkled, in fact, the flight of the population since they realised there would be no air-strikes. So this is the starting point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. Tell us, please, who was the chief investigator of the UN from the very beginning?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean chief investigator of the UN?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you the chief investigator at that point in time? Was somebody else the chief investigator before you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have started the investigation as an investigation -- as an investigator who was part of another team, but all the other members of that team continued their work on Sarajevo. So I was the only permanent member of this non-existing team. For a while I was assisted by colleagues who were in other teams but who, to help me during specific missions, went with me during these missions, then returned after the mission to their usual activity, and the team started to look a little bit as a real team. At the end of the year 1996 when after one and a half year, at least a legal advisor was tasked to assist me in this activity. And also beginning of 1996, one investigator was detached from his team to assist me also full time, and later, I don't remember what date that was, I turned from investigator to -- to team leader. So that was the beginning of the real team for Srebrenica. That was in -- that was in 1997, I think. Before that there was no -- no dedicated team for the Srebrenica case within the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us when these rumours started, when you heard them for the first time, the rumours that had to be checked then?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I call these rumours because they were not based on -- on facts -- I mean facts. They were based on testimonies collected by journalists, but there was not at the very beginning possibility of corroboration. This is why I named these things rumours, but it was press articles in several if not all the newspapers at that -- at that time, that due to the experience some of these journalists had from Vukovar to Srebrenica, they had a personal opinion that these missing persons were not somewhere in detention. This is what the families of these victims believed until -- until at least mid-2006 but that they -- these persons were most certainly dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: When was it the first time that you heard this information or rumours? When was the first time that you, as a team -- or, rather, the UN was intrigued by this figure of 8.000? If it wasn't on the 11th of July at midday, 12.00, as you said on page 23977, when was it then?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: For sure it couldn't be on the 11th. When, I could not say. I don't have the souvenir of this press articles, but it was in the following date. It was most certainly as soon as the people arrived, so as soon as the 16th the decision to send someone there was done very quickly. No, I'm wrong, because -- no, it's after the -- it should be the 14, once the final evacuation was conducted and the people already arrived in Bosnian-held territory. Anyhow, around these dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that these rumours started in 1993? Or more specifically, are you aware of the fact that Izetbegovic disclosed to his associates that Clinton had said to him that NATO could not go to war unless the Serbs were to enter Srebrenica and slaughter 5.000 Muslims? His associate said that they did not want to sacrifice 5.000 Muslims. Were you aware of the fact that this story goes back to 1993?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Do you know the name of Tim Butcher?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never heard.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: On the 24th of July, were you in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I hope that we're going to get the text by the end of the examination. Please take a look at what Tim Butcher wrote from Tuzla in his newspaper, the "Daily Telegraph" on the 24th of July: [In English] "After five days of interviews, the United Nations chief investigator into alleged human rights abuses during the fall of Srebrenica has not found any first-hand witnesses of atrocities."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If Mr. Karadzic is reading from the article, maybe we could get it and put it on the ELMO so that we can all see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: My assumption was that he didn't get it so far, but do you have a copy of that article, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're right. Our team is trying to get a hold of that article and download it, and I believe we'll receive it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I would like to know who the chief UN investigator was in Tuzla on the 24th of July. Was it you?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Is his report correct, namely that on the 24th of July, there are no first-hand witnesses?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, his report is uncorrect for the simple reason that though we had indeed already accessed interesting -- very interesting witnesses by then, I would never have told that to this journalist whose name I -- I don't know and I probably maybe even never met. I don't know if he says that he met me when I said that, but it's his -- his assessment that at that time we had no witnesses. There were several reports from some journalists reporting about even the missions we were doing later in 1996 and who were writing things that had more or less nothing to do with what we were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know the name of Hubert Wieland?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You don't know that he was the personal representative of the High Commissioner for Human Rights and that he was present in Tuzla at the time? You were not aware of his presence or of his team? And you didn't know that he was doing something over there, too; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. And -- I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Once we've received the text, we're going to see what it says there. Do you agree -- actually, do you agree, did you know that the High Commissioner for Human Rights sent a mission there?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The High Commissioner for Human Rights has a specific mission. The ICTY has another mission, and I was not connected with this High Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please. This is what I'd be interested in. How did this happen -- or, rather, what happened with this figure, these figures, because that is of crucial importance here, the numbers game. How did this figure change? On the 24th of July, the High Commissioner for Human Rights and his representative do not have this information, and they say that they talked to a vast number of refugees who arrived in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I missed maybe something. I don't see any -- what should I do now? What number should I comment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I also don't see any basis for the suggestion that the High Commissioner for Human Rights didn't have this information. I think Mr. Karadzic simply asked if Mr. Ruez knew who this person was. I think if there's going to be any more questions along this line, we should see the article that he's referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please reformulate your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Independently of Mr. Wieland and the High Commissioner for Human Rights who was in Tuzla at the same time and asking questions of the same persons that the OTP was questioning, from those first rumours onwards, how did this number of victims in Srebrenica change? You can tell us this: Where does this first information originate from, the first figure of victims in Srebrenica? And you talk about newspapers too. Were they your source of information or was it the other way round. Were you and your Prosecutions, the Office of the Prosecutor, their source of information?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Two questions in here, one being the base number, the ICRC book of missing persons. I think it could be quite easy to find from the ICRC when this book came out with these figures. As I corrected, when I talk now from at that time these 8.000, this number was not out by then. It came out much later. At that time there was no figure. It was thousands of people -- of men were missing. Thousands of men were missing, but how many thousands was not known by then. The other question is if the journalists or the Office of the Prosecutor informed the other one or all together, the answer is very simple. We did never inform the press about anything, but -- and it is at the honour of the press -- I named sometimes the press, due to the lack of investigators in the team, the additional investigation task force. The reason is that not only did some journalist directly come to us in order to provide information, but also we systematically checked during the -- these years the articles they were writing, because some of them were writing things obviously based on interesting witnesses, systematically adding Witness X who has never been interviewed by the ICTY and reporting important information. So in that case we would systematically try to get in contact with the witness in order to check if the journalistic view of the declarations of this witness were correct or if they were not. So all this was a -- I mean, any valid source of information was to be checked at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In the transcript of February 1st, that is to say yesterday, 23998 is the page reference, it says: [In English] [As read] "You mentioned during your testimony that Drazen Erdemovic provides the assessment figure related to Branjevo Farm. Do you think that Drazen Erdemovic is reliable and valuable source for information for what happening -- what was happening in Srebrenica and who can help D.C. in better understanding of this incident that occurred there?" [Interpretation] What is your position?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Position is simple. Regarding the figure of 1.200, it is impossible to rely on anyone who would make such an assessment. The only option possible is to here, like in many other instances, not only to exhume the primary grave - this has been done - but also to exhume the nine graves in Cancari valley that we believe are connected with the disturbance of the primary site. I don't know if yet this is done and the connection's all finalised. That's the only way to ascertain. And from there it would also, in addition, not be possible to have a full certainty since the bodies of those who have been slaughtered at the Pilica Dom of Culture have also been transported the day after to the main mass grave of Branjevo Farm. So the assessment there is 500. It's done by, in brackets, a serious security officer of the Drina Corps. This one might be a bit more reliable, but again, it's most probably an estimate. So all these figures out of the exhumation process cannot be considered reliable by no one. This is a clear fact. There was another question in your -- okay. I think -- I think I answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know that the Defence cannot cross-examine Erdemovic, and his statement has been admitted under 92 bis? You would rather examine him, wouldn't you? You would not consider him to be fully credible; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No. No. You don't have to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only corroboration of this -- okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When it comes to mass graves, was -- were photos taken of all of the mass graves together with the bodies that were discovered in them?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is something that will have to be covered by both William Haglund and Richard Wright. I was not -- I had not the possibility to be even once present in 1996 for the full exhumations conducted William Haglund, because meanwhile he was conducting his activities, I was continuously trying to find other sites, but there was on several occasions present during the exhumations conducted by Richard Wright. And what I saw from it is that indeed absolutely everything was not only photographed but there were films at the end of the day, at the beginning of the day in order to assert nothing had been tampered with during the night. The sites were also, as in 1996, guarded by military forces. So I think you will be overwhelmed with photographic documents of all these human remains at the morgue, at the sites, and everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you try and remember the photo with the highest number of bodies in it? Which photo contained the highest number of bodies? Can you remember such a photo?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see all the photos of all the sites that were exhumed. The sites that contained the most bodies, I think, were secondary graves with, for some, more than 200 bodies in it. So -- but I didn't go on this exhumation. I would not be able to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, you had all the photos at your disposal. All the photo material was at your disposal; right? And what was the highest number of bodies that you count -- that you could count in any single photo?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's true that I could have accessed all this photographic material, but I didn't spend, in fact, lose my time going through all this material since expert -- experts were doing this. They didn't need at all my assistance, and I had no -- I was not particularly keen to spend my days watching all these things. What I can add to the previous thing is that since I was systematically among the first ones who did the first dig in all these sites, I also took photos of every single of these sites before they were exhumed by the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. However, Mr. Ruez, do you agree with me that 500 bodies in one place in a mass grave is a good photo opportunity for any photographer? How come that in your book there is no single photo depicting over 20 bodies? Where are all those very impressive photos that were taken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Well, Dr. Karadzic, first of all that supposes that such photographs were taken. And secondly, it supposes that this witness can go into the mind of the photographer and analyse which photographs they chose to take and which they didn't. It seems to me you're asking an impossible question again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellency, with all due respect, the witness said that photos were taken of everything. If there is complete photo material, I want to see a photo depicting hundreds of bodies in one grave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Although I'm not the one who led these exhumations, I can provide you a beginning of an answer that will be more developed by Richard Wright. The way the exhumation teams operate is that they start with the top of the grave and then piece by piece discovered since all these remains are intertwined because they first went through inhumation, burial by heavy equipment, then were dug out by heavy equipment. So many bodies, you know, were cut in pieces, then loaded on board of trucks, then unloaded and dumped in other big holes. All this is a mixture of intertwined arms, legs, and so on, so it takes quite a while for the exhumation team to sort out all this and put them in body bags in order to then be matched piece by piece like a puzzle. All this takes time. And after human remains, the mass grave is slowly emptied until they reach the bottom of it. So it is more or less technically totally impossible to have a full picture of the entire content of such a grave. What we did in Cancari 12, I did explain it when we showed you the photograph. The film was not shown, but there is a full film that I took on that spot. It was not for court purpose when I took it. It was for education of the incoming exhumators in order to show them the entire process, the security aspect, the logistical aspect, and so on. So on this particular spot I wished to have what you wish now to see, that is indeed a picture of the entire surface of such a grave, which is not necessarily what was done on the other sites. So this one was indeed done specifically for the sake of showing how such a surface of grave looks like, but it's not the, in brackets, archaeological method that is in place for these exhumations. Richard Wright will provide you all -- all information you need or you wish to know about all these details.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we now look at image 66 in Mr. Ruez's book. Thank you. Mr. Ruez, would this have been a customary way of discovering bodies and revealing bodies, removing the topsoil before the bodies were recovered?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: So let me explain you this photograph. At the left you have a crime scene technician of the OTP. His name is John Gerns. I am the one at the right of the picture. This site is a site that we did not present during the Prosecution phase because this one is, I was told, not part of your indictment, but never mind, I can explain you the method. So this is a Nova Kasaba site. On this spot we had no archaeologist with us, no forensic expert. What we did, having learned from the method used by William Haglund during previous missions, the technique on this is indeed to find out what I said, that is multiple remains. If we find only one part of body or bodies it is not enough. It can be only one grave. We cannot do an exhumation process based on one body, so we need to show multiple bodies. So indeed we determined the perimeter of the top of the grave knowing this area from obvious signs like vegetation, for example, on the site. Grass is growing much quicker thanks to the natural fertiliser in which these men have been transformed into. You open the top. As soon as you begin to find something, you continue the work with your hands. So you give what I named the postmortem massage to the bodies, and you end up finding indeed where is the head, not confuse shoulders with the behind, taking care, not pushing too hard on the belly because things could spray at your face and fancy things like, and I don't describe you also the smell to which you get accustomed quite quickly. And once you have underlined the surface of this -- such a grave, this one obviously --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, no, don't interrupt. You asked the question. Please continue, Mr. Ruez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. A question deserves an answer, as we say. On this one, specifically, we showed the presence of six bodies on this one wearing civilian clothes, hands attached in the back with wire and things like this. But this one was then later fully exhumed. There were, I think, less than 100 bodies in this one connected with an execution that happened on the meadow in front. And these ones, the first one in the grave were shot inside the grave.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. My time is restricted, so let us focus on the question. I asked you whether this is how bodies are revealed before they are recovered and removed from the site, and when they are displayed in this way, are photos of the bodies taken?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one is a primary grave. It has not been disturbed because of the, in bracket, little number of bodies in it. So no use to disturb such a site, apparently. So these bodies are complete bodies, though in the secondary sites it's many -- many are bodies parts. This is what you want to know. Yes. And after this, we recovered the bodies with the soil we took out until the full exhumation of the site was conducted. We didn't take anybody out of this -- this grave. This was just to show the presence of multiple remains.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: A little while ago, you told us that there were six bodies in this grave, and all I can see are four bodies. What about the other two? Where are they? Where do you see them?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: On this photograph you have six bodies, but you cannot see because -- you can only see clearly four, because in fact they are on top each of another. There are additional pictures of this site that we could show, but again this presentation of this site was not done because it's not part of your indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I believe that it is, Mr. Ruez. However, it was not meant to be presented through you. Never mind that. What about these other bodies that you found? Are they deeper in the grave? Where are they?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Richard Wright is the one who fully exhumed this site. It's fully documented. No, it's not Richard Wright. It's -- hmm. I don't know. Anyhow, the person who was the -- who exhumed it will evidence -- fully document it. You will ask him these questions about the set-up of the grave. All the bodies are positioned during these exhumations with technical devices. You will see all this when the time will come to -- to show these things. I don't know if it already happened or if it will happen, but I'm not the expert for discussing the content of the graves.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, the fact is that we are searching for the alleged thousands of executed men. I insist on the photos being shown to me. I want to count them, but you can't do that. Very well. Never mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is completely disingenuous. Mr. Karadzic has hundreds, if not thousands, of photos that have been disclosed to him, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And he didn't put that question when Professor Wright was here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's correct. And he should also recall that we actually played the entire video of Cancari 12. There were photos shown of the Kozluk side. There are photos of Branjevo in Mr. Ruez's report. I think this whole line of questioning is a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Absolutely, yes, Mr. Mitchell. Thank you. Mr. Karadzic. Yes, please continue then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we knew look at photo 246, the one depicting Branjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You're familiar with this photo; right? There is no doubt that what we can see are the remains of human bodies in a state of disarray. How many bodies would you say are depicted in this photo approximately?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the exhumation report, I cannot count. I never tried to count this, how many bodies are on the surface of this stack because it's a stack, so we can really see the surface. If I remember well, it's 110 bodies that were found in one small portion of the disturbed grave of the Branjevo Farm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, before I forget, you testified about Kravica. On which one -- which side of the road is the Kravica farm building as you drive from --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Karadzic repeat the names of the places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you repeat the direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: As you drive from Konjevic Polje towards Bratunac via Kravica, on what side of the road is the farm building?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Let's make it clear that we are completely away from Branjevo, because we were at the Branjevo Farm. Now we are at -- at 60 kilometres south back to Kravica. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're correct. I'm just interested in the side of the road where that building is.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. Driving from the intersection of Konjevic Polje towards Bratunac, the building is on the right side of the road.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you know how many people were detained at the Nova Kasaba stadium?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, and it would be extremely difficult to know, because at the stadium, as in other places, people were coming in, groups then were moved out, and this process lasted. So whatever photograph we could have would only be an instant photograph. Even if we had the ability to count those seen on these instant shots, it's just an instant shot. It's not a full video of a full day, for example. So I don't know how many people were on these detention sites, the 12 and the 13 July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By the "stadium," do you mean the football field, Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I understand what he meant. Football field was talking about stadium.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we go into private session briefly?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we zoom in on this rectangle with the bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In this football pitch, they are sitting. We heard from witness statements that they are sitting, and they were guarded by several men. Do you agree that that is information we got from witness statements?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. These individuals that we see standing apart in the front, in the foreground, would those be the Serb soldiers, the guards?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Those who are grouped are prisoners. The guards would be standing around. There is no need to have a huge amount of guards on the left side, no need.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you try to assist us. I'm now counting the shortest side, one, two, three, four, five, maybe six. And the longest side, one, two, three, four, five, six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Ten, 11 at the outside; correct?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: One, two, three, four, five, till eleven, what? Centimetres, people, metres? I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Individuals, Mr. Ruez, those who are sitting. The shortest side of the rectangle. We can count five to six, and the longest side of the rectangle, we can count 10 to 11 individuals. Can you count more than I did? And when you do the arithmetic you get 60 to 70 people.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're counting skills are far better than mine. I would not even try to do such a counting, but I think any reasonable person who would take a dot as you can see some of them on -- on this photograph, would have a much, much larger number than the one you come up with. But this type of counting I never attempted and would not even attempt, because it would at the end be, anyhow, extremely fuzzy since it's material more or less impossibility. I mean, if an assessment could be made -- and we never bothered doing so, since again this is an instant photograph. It depicts a situation at an unknown, very precise time, but the situation on this soccer field most certainly changed several times during that day depending on the arrival and departure of grouped prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: You are trying to say that they left in several batches or they were transported all at once. Do you have evidence that they were transported in groups? And the moment is 1400 hours on the 14th of July.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is approximately 1400, and it is not the 14 of July. The evacuation of all these regroupment spots was --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thirteenth.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is 13. We do not know about what -- what series of event happened on this spot. We -- we don't have enough precise information on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can we talk about 1.500 to 2.000 prisoners with this length and breadth of the rectangle? And we can count the individuals more than clearly. Can we really talk about 1.500 to 2.000 prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would not say. Again, never counted them. I mean, attempted to count or estimate their number.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we now look at that document, the text by Mr. Tim Butcher from "Daily Telegraph," dated 24 July 1995. Oh, sorry, we have "The New York Times." 1D5028, please. This is another text, but could we zoom in on it. This text -- this article refers to you; correct? Do you remember it? That's after I was brought here.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I have no knowledge at all about this article. 9 August 2008, no, I've never seen this. I don't think so. "New York Times," no. I don't recall anyhow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you make any statements after I was arrested and brought here? Did you make any statements for the media?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That could be. I don't remember, but this -- this could be, yes. I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you look at paragraph 2. Do you agree that this is premature on your part to say this?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regarding the 8.000 men, it's certainly not me who puts this figure out. I constantly say that this figure is only the figure of those missing, not those assassinated, and we count only for the sake of the criminal investigation the assassinations, not those whose cause of death is unknown. The unknown causes are always considered as a legitimate combat. And for the rest, indeed the reconstruction of the scenario, I -- I could have said that, yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we scroll down, please. Look at this text. Did you make these statements, or did they make them up?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I should read all of it, but the parts I'm already reading, I abide by the words. Even if they don't necessarily come from my mouth, they are well reproduced, let's say. Yes, yes, yes. I go quickly. Aside a few purely stylistic stuff, yes. Okay. I retreat nothing from this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Ruez, doesn't this make you an unbiased witness or at least detracts from your position as an unbiased witness?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's up to the Court to decide, President Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could we see 1 page further.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Look what you say here: [In English] "I signed it -- signed up immediately." [Interpretation] In reckoning that this is all praiseworthy, did you display a similar enthusiasm for investigating the suffering of Serbs, and do you have any findings about that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The thing is that when you arrive at the OTP, you never know in which branch you will be working. As you might know, the organisation is such that you have teams working on the cases where Serbs were victims, where Bosniaks were victims, where Croats were victims. You do not select in which of these three branches you will operate. Had I worked on a case where the victims had been Serbs, I would most certainly and without any doubt on my side have put the same energy finding the truth about what had happened to them, but the story was a bit different. As I had explained, I ended up, nearly at random, ended up being the head of this specific investigation, and I did only this during all my time of presence in -- nearly only this during all my time of presence at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, having read the document now, do you -- does it jog your memory as to whether or not you gave that interview?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I did absolutely, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: You did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I also will never hide the fact that even during my time here as a -- as a member of the OTP, I gave already at that time many interviewed -- interviews. I was cleared to do so by the Prosecution. I also accompanied the press people, and I -- when I left the Tribunal, I said I'm leaving the Tribunal, I'm not leaving the case. Meaning that since there was still ongoing propaganda denying even the existence of the crime that was committed, I felt also as my duty to continue this part of what, for me, is indeed a full part of the activity once I -- once I have left this place. And I would never have stopped until the arrest of both President Karadzic and mainly General Ratko Mladic, who was, in fact, the real target of the investigation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Excellency.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, you've just said that there was a lot of propaganda and denial. Did you take into account the propaganda of exaggeration, of overblowing? Did you take into account the propaganda against the Serbs that hyperbolised the numbers? Did you notice such things going on?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. The -- my first concern when I arrived in Tuzla in summer 1995 was indeed the risk of falling in a trap of propaganda on all sides. So when I said that the recommendation of Mr. Akashi, I didn't know about it, but when he said cautious about the numbers, it's certainly not only about the numbers that we had to be cautious. We had to be cautious about any type of information we would receive. The war was still going on, and since a big famous one, we all know that propaganda is a weapon of war. So this was a risk.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, is it time for the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We will very have a break for 30 minutes, and after which you will have about 40 minutes to conclude your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Could we please have 1D5031. sorry, can I tender the document that's there? The witness confirmed that he gave that interview, that he did talk to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise to Mr. Mitchell for the late notification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that's admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2049, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit 1D5031. My apologies once again. And then can we have page 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let us see what this is about first.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If we look at the first page, we can see what it is. It is a document listing media topics pertaining to Srebrenica. [In English] Could you show the whole page and then next.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Who -- who is the author, or who compiled this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: This is a site that is dealing with Srebrenica, Srebrenica Historic Project. [Interpretation] But the quotes are correct, and all the sources are correctly cited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, my first question is why -- why you do not provide the original cite, original news clipping, for example, "Economist." Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can just clarify one thing. Is the Srebrenica Historic Project, that's the web site run by Stevan Karganovic; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know who runs it, but I know that it quotes specific texts in specific papers, but we can obtain all of these texts, although we're going to need time for that. I just wanted to show this witness the last page because it has to do with Tuzla in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Let us proceed and see what happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at this. There's a reference to Mr. Hubert Wieland here, and there is a quote from the "Daily Telegraph" on the 24th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What is the question, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: What can you say about this, that on the 24th of July, another UN agency in charge of refugees presented this information; namely, that there aren't any first-hand witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The answer is simple. As I said, Mr. -- who I don't know -- I mean, the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights has a mission. I don't know what is exactly his mission, but what I can say is we have another mission. It was in the frame of a criminal investigation by the ICTY, and -- I mean, if he did not find any relevant witness, be sure that we did. And not only we, because one of the survivors at the Orahovac site at that time already was given -- was giving, sorry, at that time interviews even to the press, not only to officials. I can give you the name of this witness if you wish.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Perhaps he's protected, but actually, if he spoke to the papers, not really.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This one did at that time, and even was -- I mean, he was -- he is a protected witness, but at that time he gave interviews with his full name. I could only give his code-name for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We'll leave it there. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I was going to say, Mr. President, perhaps we shouldn't give his code-name, because that would then link that to who was giving interviews at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, do you see the reasons for my concern about this enthusiasm and fanaticism of the policeman who conducted the investigations? This is a UN agency as well. That is why I showed you that interview given to "Monitor" and I asked you whether you were enthusiastic not to say fanatical in your approach to this problem.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The lack of any type of evidence from this report is indeed obvious, but again the mission of this UN High Commissioner and the mission we had was significantly different. So I cannot comment on this. I don't even know if this information came out from the UN or if it is a report for -- from a journalist who was just not informed about what this UN commissioner could find out. There was another person who arrived in the area at the same time than we did, since we were in the same helicopter flying from Split to Tuzla. It was Mr. Mazowiecki. And Mr. Mazowiecki, he had access to witnesses, including one who claimed having survived a mass execution, and Mr. Mazowiecki, upon return, resigned from his UN mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this acceptable, Excellencies, this last page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I don't know what probative value it will have even if it is to be admitted. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would object to this without some more information about the source of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll not admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the interview in the French parliament be admitted, 20506? That's the 65 ter number. And the witness confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, that will be admitted.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit D2050, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In relation to those questions that had to do with photographs and numbers, I was quite clumsy in putting them. I would like to deal with it more simply now. Mr. Ruez, you relied on witness statements, especially injured parties. You also took into account media accounts. You were relying on pathologists' reports. I wanted to ask you the following: Did you study the photographs that are available, and did you check by counting the bodies in these photographs the other sources that you had?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, we didn't take in account any media reports. What I said is that one -- when a media report reported an information that could be useful for the investigation, we did ever -- everything we could to check the information, but we never acted. I mean, we never have used any media account for this investigation aside this aspect. For the rest, in terms of counting bodies or assessing bodies based on photographs, I explained already that those photographs that show groups of people, we never -- I never made any attempt to count. First of all, because it could only bring an assessment of numbers, and the main reason is also that these are instant shots. So it's impossible to conclude for certain that the situation at an hour, a minute, second, is not going to change completely one hour later. So no counting for these. Also in terms of counting bodies on photographs, that was absolutely none of my business. There were experts in that matter, and they were not counting the bodies based on photographs but with other methods that were explained by these experts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: In the Krstic case, on page 501, you spoke about attempts to get to the buses. Do you have that statement of yours? 501, that's the page reference. Did you receive this information to the effect that there was a race as to who would find a seat on the bus to Kladanj as fast as possible?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a hard copy that could be given to the witness. We're talking about a completely different site now, so --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in Potocari, I think. I can answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, then very well. Page -- yes. Please continue then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Indeed, due to -- we didn't enter these details for this presentation, but indeed due to the ambiance of terror that was generated by the Serb soldiers in Potocari, people there were indeed very eager to get on board of one of the buses that was doing this transfer towards Kladanj. The thing -- the thing is that to board the buses, the people had first to go through a line of Serb soldiers who were separating the men from the women and the children and took them to the first detention centre that was the so-called white house from where then these prisoners were taken to Bratunac. But indeed due to the crimes that were committed during the 12 and the 13 in Bratunac, yes, it's true that the people were extremely in a hurry to leave this place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, were you there --

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, not in Bratunac, in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Were you there, or did you infer that on the basis of the film that you had available?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The knowledge we have about the situation in Potocari comes from, let's say, one part of the investigation that focused only on the events in Potocari. So based not only on the film, which is a very important piece of it since it's images taken on the spot at the time of the events, but also from all the witnesses in the -- in that -- in this location, these being not only the Bosniaks who were evacuated, but also all the UN personnel who was witnessing what was going on there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: So what is the crime that you refer to in Potocari? What was the reason for this panic? First of all, do you see this panic on the film itself?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He didn't testify as -- as a crime base witness. Your legal advisor objected to the substantive evidence he was asked about, and now you are inviting him to comment upon what he heard from witnesses. His evidence in Krstic was not admitted in this trial. He may well be allowed to comment upon what he heard from witnesses, but in this case he didn't. I don't see the point of your questions, but that said, it's up to you to ask any questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise. I confused two witnesses. I thought that this had been admitted, too, in this case. But now we're just relying on viva voce, right, what the witness himself said?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Then I'm going to move on to another topic. Please neglect this. 1D5026, could we have that, please? That's a video that was announced by the Prosecution, and then they gave up on it. Could we now view it from 6:04 to 6:44.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is this part of trial video, Mr. Mitchell?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: One second, Mr. President. I'll confirm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, it is. It's part one of the trial video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see 8:43 to 8:54.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Can you stop for a moment. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The transcript of this is on ERN 07047813 in the trial video took. It's in the section entitled "Srebrenica town 10 July 1995."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Ruez, that from 6:04 to 6:44 this footage you can see the presence of the Muslim army that is firing from the town of Srebrenica itself?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember indeed these pictures, but for the rest I -- I don't know the name of the man here in the middle of the screen, but, yes, he's one of the commanders of the 28th Division. Yes, for sure. The -- this is next to Company Bravo, the UN battalion. That's the sub-base. The main base was in Potocari. This one is in Srebrenica town. This is just probably just a few -- before Srebrenica town is evacuated with these two directions we have explained.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you remember having seen a scene where the Muslim army firing from the town of Srebrenica itself?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the footage at one moment there is indeed a mortar nearby who is firing rounds towards the Serb positions, indeed, yeah, uh-huh.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Can we now look at 8:43 to 8:54, and could this footage also be admitted from 6:04 to 6:44, what the witness confirmed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see that this witness speaks of 15.000 inhabitants who are to defend themselves? Fifteen thousand inhabitants, and he is cursing and saying they should defend themselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The transcript doesn't say any such thing. It says "15.000 inhabitants, fuck," that's it. Nothing about, "defend yourselves."

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Let's play it again. Let's see whether he says that there are 15.000 inhabitants there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MORRISON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, you described him as a witness. He's not a witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. This part of the film displays the following: This commander, who is trying to organise the defence, as the witness confirmed, says that there are 15.000 inhabitants there, and he is calling for a defence -- or, rather, trying to organise some kind of defence. We can view this half minute.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He says: "Cowards."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we have transcript for that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can that be seen now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see it, Mr. Witness, that he's trying to organise the defence, and he is claiming that there are 15.000 inhabitants there, and he's calling them cowards because they're not fighting?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand B/C/S, so I don't have any live -- I mean, I cannot hear what he's saying. There is a transcript on it. I don't know if the Prosecution considers this transcript as being an official transcript. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: One clarifying question for you, Mr. Mitchell. Have we not admitted the trial video in its entirety?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So this part is already in the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. They didn't want to show it. That's why I thought that I should show it. Can we now look at 1D5207. And can we start at 44:10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This is also part of the trial video, the first part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm not -- we are not seeing anything. Yes. But could you identify the page number of the transcript as well, last four digits?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: As soon as I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- see the start of it I'll be able to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you display 44:10 to 44:35.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is enough. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you see how -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go on, Mr. Mitchell. You wanted to say something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It won't be necessary. We saw it already, didn't we?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I just wanted to give you the transcript page. It ends in 7828.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that the meeting between Lieutenant-Colonel Karremans and General Mladic took place in the evening on the 11th July and that it took place at the Fontana Hotel?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. This first meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that at the end of the day on the 11th of July, Lieutenant Karremans says that there are about 10.000 refugees in his base?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that moment they were not in the base. Only approximately 5.000 could be accommodated in the base, and the number he talks about is the number of those who had arrived on -- in the evening of the 11. The situation then inflated in terms of numbers. But again, these numbers are assessments, and since I didn't answer the question regarding the previous footage, my interpretation of what this 28th Division commander says is that he's referring to the number of able men. He's not talking about the women and the children and the elderly and the disabled, because these ones are not supposed to take weapons to defend themselves. So this 15.000 will be probably the amount of those who ended up gathering at the north-west of the enclave east -- west, sorry, yes, Susnjari -- no, in the location from where then they took off from the enclave to the woods.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: However, we know the division had about 15.000 men, but he doesn't say that. He says 15.000 inhabitants; right?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The transcript says "inhabitants," but then the question is does he also counts in this the women, children, and the elderly, claiming that they are cowards and should defend themselves. I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Do you agree that some order should be installed in the system of numbers relative to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I fully agree with you. This is why the only number that counts for a criminal case is the number of people who have been assassinated in this extermination of prisoners. This is the only number that, at the end of the day, counts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. However, when it comes to the so-called deportation, do you agree that it is also necessary to establish how many inhabitants were there, how many arrived in Tuzla, and why they arrived there, whose will was it for them to arrive there?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The legal term for this aspect is foreseeable transfer, if I remember well. The number of these is known more or less, more or less. You had the document of the UN that was numbering these people according to the numbers in the refugee centres in Tuzla, in and around Tuzla, but you were right. Many were accommodated in places where they were not counted. So this number is a minimum number. Then, you know, everything is -- what's the starting base of the calculation? You know, you -- you pulled out a number that was an assessment of 93. Was this a correct number? Was it not a correct number? All these numbers will, anyhow, be extremely fuzzy. We do not count for the criminal case, possible also disappearances during the trip from Potocari to Kladanj, because it's impossible to investigate, and the numbers would be too small to enable any serious investigation, though we had indications that this might have happened. So -- but I said several times since the beginning of this testimony the only number that can be considered as relevant for the criminal investigation is the number of people found in graves that we can connect with the place and cause of death. So people who were in detention and were executed. At this stage, as I said, my knowledge post facto, because I have left the place since 2001, is that at this stage some -- a bit more than 6.000 individuals have been identified by name from these graves, and these men were missing from Srebrenica July 1995, not 1992, 1993, 1994. July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Ruez. We will prove that there were all the different years according to Muslim sources, which we are not going to present today. Are you saying that among those people, among those who were identified, there is nobody who died in any other day -- any other way, for example, during combat? We've already been through that. We had people who testified here and who said that they'd seen four or five people being killed around them, being killed in combat, and still they are in the database of those who were exhumed from the mass graves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: First, Mr. President, that's a statement. There is no question. And second, I don't think there's any evidence from a witness I've seen that people were killed in combat and were then exhumed from the mass graves, certainty the mass graves that are related or charged in our indictment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wish to add something on this, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Several members of 1st Zvornik Brigade have been indicted and trialed at the ICTY, among them Dragan Obrenovic, the second in command of the Zvornik Brigade who pleaded guilty. Among them also Major Jokic, who was the head of the engineer battalion of the Zvornik Brigade. Strangely, none of these two most knowledgeable persons about what is called the "cleaning of the terrain" process has ever, ever claimed having even witnessed the fact that bodies had been taken from battle-fields to be reburied in these graves that the Zvornik Brigade has opened and filled. So I'm honestly quite astonished that such a theory that has never been put up front by all this most knowledgeable persons in charge of such a process comes up as a possibility, because these ones are not Bosniak or whatever victims. They are those who committed the crimes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And those who made arrangements with the OTP, at least one of them who plea bargained, that is?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The one who took his full responsibility, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Do you know that sanitisation is not carried out by the military but by the civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe, but then to touch one of these sites that were under full control of the army where not even the police could approach would be a very, very strange move from these civilians of civil protection to step on the goods of the army at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: How do you explain that Witness 045 mentioned the names of some six or seven people who were killed next to him in combat, they were not executed, and still their DNAs are in the database and we're also charged with their murders? I was able to check their names against the names of their parents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, this was something that I think we addressed either yesterday or the day before. Witness 045 is the dam survivor. Here he was talking about bodies who -- or people who were killed in combat prior to him being arrested. It's a totally separate thing from the execution and burial that he later witnessed at the dam.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. He didn't say that they were found in the mass graves, did he?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Not specifically, Mr. President, but he said, "we're also charged with their murders," which I think the clear implication is then that they came out of those mass graves, because Mr. Karadzic is not charged with killings of surface remains which were recovered from that area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Now it's time for you to wrap up your cross-examination, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I could like to call up just one more photo, but before that, six or seven names that 045 mentioned as people who were killed next to him, they -- they are in the DNA's database as those who were executed, and it will be -- to prove that. I'm asking the witness whether he is aware of such things happening, and we will be able to find as many as up to 40 per cent of those who died in different places, who were killed in different ways.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's just an argument. I think it's time to conclude. Unless you have a specific question, I'll conclude, I'll put your cross-examination to an end.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Photo 260.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: And can you explain on page 57 -- I believe that that was on page 57 when you said that this photo depicts the first layer. Can you explain the meaning of the first layer? Is there another layer of soil between the first layer and the second layer?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This junk of bodies has the full size of the mound that you can see on the picture. So it's not soil. It's what is left of the human beings that have been dumped in this large hole. The entire -- the entire depth of this initial hole is covered with bodies, with soil mixed with it and shell casings mixed with it. So you have here the size of the grave, and what to say more? The picture is self-explanatory, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, my question was this: On page 57, you said this was the first layer. Here we see a skull that belonged to one of the bodies above it, and there is about 20 centimetres of soil between the skull and the rest of the remains. How can you explain this, that there are layers of bodies and there are layers of soil between those layers of bodies. How can this fact be explained unless all those bodies were buried in different stages, in different phases, at different times?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a question for the archaeologists who dug the bodies out of these graves. They didn't dug them out, by the way. They dealt with them like they do with the 2- or 3.000-year-old objects that they find in other type of activities that they normal conduct. I won't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Then you cannot answer the question whether new bodies were added on top of the other bodies in a mass grave at some subsequent times.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know what I think about this theory, so I leave it to scientists to sort it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. Thank you. I apologise for insisting on precision, but I'm sure you will appreciate that as a police officer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, there's five areas that I'd like to briefly address with you. You were asked earlier today some questions about the number of prisoners at Nova Kasaba on the 13th of July, and Mr. Karadzic suggested to you at around page 23 of today's transcript that you could only see 60 to 70 people on that aerial image that was taken at approximately 1400 hours on the 13th of July. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I please have Exhibit P168 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, what you can see -- or if you can take your time and read this document.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can scroll down.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Uh-huh. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And go over to the next page in English.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yep, crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go back to the first page in English now. And this was a report sent from the IKM or the forward command post of the 65th Protection Regiment at 1400 hours on the 13 July. It states in the very first sentence that there are over 1.000 members of the former 28th Division of the so-called BiH Army captured in the area of Dusanovo Kasaba. And then at least a proposal from the assistant commander for security and intelligence to prohibit access to unauthorised individuals, prohibit traffic for United Nations vehicles and then place these prisoners indoor or in an area protected from sighting from the ground or the air. And my question, Mr. Ruez, is: Firstly, does this number of 1.000 -- over 1.000 members, is that consistent with the information that your investigation uncovered?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, it's a very risky game to play with numbers. I would easily have added a zero to the assessment done by President Karadzic based on the photograph, but again, I would not do such a thing. Having this number officially by the document you are showing is for sure the best way to have an assessment, and at the time and the hour of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And we see at point 3, the proposal from the assistant commander for security and intelligence affairs of the VRS Main Staff was to place these prisoners indoors or in an area protected from sighting from the ground or the air. Is that what actually happened to these prisoners?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, two things happened, one being -- there were -- there were not many places to put the people indoors aside the Kravica warehouse, the little warehouse at the intersection of Konjevic Polje. But I'm not sure I have to mention that, but then there was the request of transfer of the packets from Bratunac to warehouses north, and that was a communication that Miroslav Deronjic had, and he explained to me what packets meant, and [Overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell, I'm not sure --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Mr. Ruez. I'm not sure whether this arises from the cross-examination. You can move on to your next topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The next area I'd like to ask you about, Mr. Ruez, is yesterday at transcript page 24047, you were asked about an aerial image of Branjevo Farm that's dated 17 July 1995. This is one of the images in your book. Page 219 in the hard copy. And what -- what you said about this image was the process is ending at this moment. There are still bodies left on the surface. The grave is not closed yet, but this inhumation was completed according to the Engineer Unit's log. Inhumation was completed that day. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I look at 65 ter 2158, and it's page 17 in the English and page 137 in the B/C/S. Do you recognise what this document is?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, if you can look at --

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean, I know it's probably the document I was referring to, but I'm not hundred per cent sure. I would think so, yes. The work at Branjevo, the work with the ULT, the ULT being a digger. Yes, that's the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So is this points 2, 3, and 5 that we can see that are related to what we can see on the aerial image?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 2 and 3, yes. Sorry, the 5 also, yes, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, yesterday and also today you were asked some questions about the estimate of 1.200 prisoners killed at Branjevo Farm, and that was based on the estimation of Drazen Erdemovic. And yesterday at transcript 23998, Mr. Karadzic said to you: "Could you get anything more objective and impartial than Drazen Erdemovic? Could you not deal with it more scientifically, if you will?" Do you recall that series of questions?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. The answer was not fully complete, but I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can I go to 65 ter 23953.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for an explanation? What's this BG 2 and LT?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I will allow the witness to explain it if he knows. BGH-700 and ULT 220.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The two are heavy equipment diggers, front loader.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It doesn't have anything to do with the number of victims; right? These figures are not related to the number of victims.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic, it's not an appropriate comment. I'm told that the Registry can't --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Karadzic. The Registry told me that it can't open the document you referred to by that number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I just wanted a complete answer. What are these references and names, these acronyms and numbers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
