utterances.text: I can respond to that. Mr. Karadzic is no doubt aware that the evidence of the excavator driver who drove the BGH-700 is actually in evidence in this case, Cvijetin Ristanic. The platoon commander of the Engineering Company, Dejan Lazarevic, his testimony is also in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: By way of 92 bis, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Correct. And those two witnesses give a full explanation of the burials at Branjevo Farm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm still not satisfied. Is this number something related --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- to the brand, the type, or the number of victims?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I find your intervention even obstructive this time. Yes, Mr. Mitchell. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The 65 ter number I wanted was 23593.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, this is a document that you haven't seen before. It's entitled "Update to the Summary of Forensic Evidence ...," and it's dated the 13th of January, 2012. If I can go to page 40 in e-court. And just look at the very first sentence there which gives an explanation at the data that we're about to see. "The table below presents the total number of individuals identified per mass execution site - primary and corresponding secondary graves linked to these sites." If we can go then to the next page and scroll down to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about leaving it to Mr. Dusan Janc when he comes? Is Mr. Ruez capable of commenting on his evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I can leave it to when Mr. Janc comes, but I think this number provided by Drazen Erdemovic was specifically challenged, and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't you proceed then. Move on to your next topic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Ruez, I'd like to deal briefly with the issue of combat casualties, and if I can refer to transcript page 24024, lines 8 to 10. Yesterday Mr. Karadzic suggested to you that the combat casualties in the Bare area had been buried in the graves that you investigated. Do you recall that series of questions?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do. And initially I didn't know that he was talking about the area north of Kravica. I thought he was talking about an area much closer to -- I mean, to an eventual possibility, though it was not the case. It was an area where the Sapna thumb is, so in the area of Orahovac. But I didn't relies at that point he was talking about the surface remains at Bare who had been buried by no one before Elizabeth Rehn came with a team to collect surface remains which are not connected with our criminal investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So to be crystal clear, those remains were still on the surface in 1996, and obviously were not buried in the graves that you investigated.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, and I even think that after this first process there were still bodies on the -- on the surface in this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Did your investigation find any evidence that on 13, 14, 15, 16, or 17 July the Bosnian Serb forces or civil protection went into these areas where surface remains were found in 1996 and collected some surface remains and left some behind?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one among all those we talked during the investigation, no one ever came up with such an information, though indeed it would have been of the interest of the Serb side to bring such an information if it would be a valid one so in order to create a haze around the origin the bodies that could still be found, knowing that the goal of the entire disturbance operation was to hide the bodies so that they would never be found. It's, in my eyes, absolute nonsense to claim that additional bodies have been put in these graves. It doesn't make any sense to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ruez. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask for a small clarification?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you put the question, on what item do you like to ask a question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the existence of a separate grave for Bare as the witness claimed and I denied, a special separate grave for those fallen; and secondly, regarding exaggeration and inflation of numbers. We saw that on the video footage where somebody says, yes, there are exaggerations concerning the number of prisoners.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, Mr. Karadzic. You dealt with those issued and nothing arises from the re-examination of Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I have one question, Mr. Ruez. Shall we upload Exhibit P4269, which is a panorama montage of Kravica warehouse from the clips of Mr. Petrovic's video. Probably you remember that I put a question to you. It's transcript page T23775, and I reminded you there that you said: "At the entrance, at the front west of the warehouse where one can see a Bosnian Serb soldier just in front at the right hand, the picture and a stack of dead bodies or people, who most probably tried to exit the place once the shooting started and who are piled up at the entrance." You remember that testimony you gave?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember very well, but the strange thing is that on the screen we never had this full picture. We only had the one-third totally at the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, this is a composite, but you have --

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I made the composite, so indeed I know this picture quite well, but it was not the one we had on the screen. We couldn't see the bus also. It's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Mitchell, could you tell me the page number -- page number of the close-up of the west side? Yes, it's page 111 and onwards. And I also asked you as to the door, and you said, I quote: "I would think there has never been a door. It's an open space." Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If I were to put to you now that there used to be a door and it was closed at the time and what it looked -- what looked like windows on this picture were actually metal door handle.

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No way. No, no. What we see at the back is one of the windows that leads to the outside at the back of the warehouse. This is a full open space. The frame of this door -- I mean door opening, sorry, was found at the Glogova, the mass grave site, as well as a piece of concrete that matches a missing part of this warehouse. But there was no door, especially not at this moment where the bodies are piled in the front but also more deep inside or the entire place at this moment was certainly covered with bodies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Before going further with the witness, Mr. Mitchell, Mr. Tieger, do you have position in relation to this issue as to the door?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, as you know, this was a topic of much conjecture in the last case, and I think we didn't contest the Defence's position that there was a door. I'm not sure I would go as far as to say that we agree there's a door, but if I can confer and maybe come back to you after the next break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. So you heard the position of the Prosecution, but if you were -- I were to tell you that there was a door which was closed at the time, would that -- would your observation or conclusion be different from what you said earlier on?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I would not change my position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. And further, yesterday's transcript page 23993, and you said that when Mr. Petrovic and Borovcanin arrived, the killing was still ongoing. Do you remember having said that?

utterances.speaker: JEAN-RENE RUEZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON

utterances.text: I'd now like to read a summary of the witness's evidence. On 11 July 1995, after the fall of Srebrenica, the witness and his family left their home. The witness's family went to Potocari, and the witness went to Jaglici as he was afraid of being killed by Serb soldiers. There were around 10- to 15.000 people at Jaglici who decided to head to Tuzla. The witness left on the afternoon of 12 July but was captured by Serb soldiers near Nova Kasaba at around 7.00 a.m. on 13 July. He was taken first to the elementary school in Nova Kasaba. Then at around 2.00 p.m., he was taken to a football pitch just outside Nova Kasaba where he saw 1.500 to 2.000 Muslim men sitting in rows surrounded by armed Serb soldiers. After a while General Mladic came to the football pitch and told the Muslim men that they would be exchanged and ordered that a list of their names be made. While Mladic was present, one prisoner was beaten and shot to death by the Serb soldiers, but Mladic did not respond in any way. In the late afternoon, buses came and drove the prisoners to Bratunac. Near Sandici, the witness saw a group of men surrounded by Serb soldiers. Further on, near Kravica, the witness saw a hangar on the right of the road with four or five dead bodies at the entrance. He also heard shooting from behind the hangar. The bus stopped for the night in Bratunac. The witness heard shooting throughout the night and four or five people were taken off the bus and never came back. On 14 July, the prisoners remained on the bus in Bratunac. That afternoon, a soldier told the prisoners they were going to be exchanged and then the bus, along with four or five others, drove north to the school in Pilica. When the buses arrived at the Pilica school, the prisoners were ordered to enter the school gym which later filled up completely. The witness also saw people sitting and standing on the stairs leading to the first floor of the school. Later that night, the witness and four other men volunteered to get water. They took buckets and went outside, past the football field and a tower to a water point with two fountains. As the men started to fill up the buckets, the witness heard a bus approach the school followed by the sound of shooting and people crying for help. The guard ordered them to return to the gym as quickly as possible. The next day, 15 July, Serb soldiers took jewellery, watches and money from the men in the gym. That night, men were also taken out of the gym and some did not return. On the morning of 16 July 1995, the prisoners were told that the young men were to be exchanged. As the witness left the gym, his hands were tied together behind his back. Three buses were parked outside the gym and the witness climbed onto the second bus. Once these three buses were full, they drove toward a meadow where the witness saw many dead bodies. He then watched as men were taken off the first bus in groups of ten, escorted by three or four soldiers to the meadow where the other dead bodies were and then shot individually and killed. The witness's bus was next. He was in the third group that was taken from the bus. He walked to the meadow where the other bodies were and was ordered to stop. There, a group of ten Serb soldiers shot at the prisoners from automatic rifles and an M-84 machine-gun. The witness threw himself face down on the ground as they opened fire and another dead prisoner fell across his head. The witness then heard soldiers being given an order to shot people individually. He was shot in the back, but the bullet passed under his left armpit and through his shirt and he was only scratched. The witness testified that groups of prisoners continued to be brought to that meadow and killed for approximately four more hours into the afternoon. That evening a vehicle arrived and unloaded more bodies at the site. The witness spent the night in the killing field and the next day under a bridge. From his hiding place, he heard the sounds of machines working all day. He met an older man, and they escaped together but eventually turned themselves in when they became exhausted. The witness was then taken to the Batkovic camp and finally released on 26 December 1995.
